estimates.note: Holybro's pin map doesn't number the pins, so the battery end is taken as pin 1: check one with a meter. The ESC's own idle draw isn't published, so 50 mA is a guess, and 12 V (4S at 3.0 V a cell) is taken as the bottom of its range
ARK doesn't publish its supplies' efficiencies; 85% is a guess for small buck converters at these currents. ARK also doesn't say whether the CAN port is terminated

The draw is Matek's figure for its ELRS-R24, which has the same ESP8285 and SX128x chips: 40 to 45 mA before binding, 70 to 75 mA bound, 90 to 95 mA in WiFi mode (https://www.mateksys.com/?portfolio=elrs-r24). 4.5 to 5.5 V is an assumed range around RadioMaster's 5 V. The 3.3 V logic level is inferred from the ESP8285, which runs on 2.7 to 3.6 V
The plug is 6-pin on a 1.25 mm pitch per a retailer's cable listing. Benewake doesn't name the family, so it's taken as GH-compatible
ARK doesn't say whether the ARK FPV terminates its CAN port. If it does, R_FC comes off, or the bus has three terminators

The pin list follows Adafruit's usual breakout layout (VIN, 3Vo, GND, SCL/SCK, SDA/MOSI, DO/MISO, CS, INT1, INT2); the product page only names some of them. The draw and its 3 to 5.5 V range are guesses

The board's pin order isn't published, so the pins are listed by function. It has two 1 kOhm resistors near the chip whose job isn't documented: if they pull IN or EN up rather than down, the board would hand the motors to the Teensy by default, so the build package says to check them with a meter and the design adds its own pull-downs. The supply draw is a guess that allows for a power LED
Pololu shows efficiency as curves; 80% is a round figure, and at the microamps these switches take, the quiescent current is what really counts
ARK gives 5 V and no range, so 4.75 to 5.25 V is assumed. The second CAN plug passes the 5 V straight on to the next node; its limit is taken as the JST-GH contact's 1 A

Typical is the 8 W the sizing model assumes (software video encoding keeps the CPU busy) and worst is Jeff Geerling's 9.8 W under stress-ng on the 4 GB board (https://www.jeffgeerling.com/blog/2024/new-2gb-pi-5-has-33-smaller-die-30-idle-power-savings/), both at 5.1 V. The 4.63 V floor is the undervoltage warning and 5.25 V is USB's ceiling: Raspberry Pi doesn't publish a range for the GPIO 5 V pins, or describe powering through them. The camera supply's rating and efficiency are guesses, and so is the fan header's pin order

Raspberry Pi's figure for its case fan, about 60 mA at 5 V, stands in for typical, and the Pi 4 case fan's 0.18 A rating for the worst case. The pin order is a guess, and 4.5 to 5.5 V an assumed range

250 mA is taken as the draw at 3.3 V on the camera connector, 300 mA as the worst case, and 3.1 to 3.5 V as its range: all guesses, since Raspberry Pi publishes nothing specific to the Camera Module 3

Typical is 212 mA (2 MHz at 21 dBm, transmitting nonstop, the conservative case for video) and 4.5 to 5.5 V is an assumed range. These are the V1 card's numbers. The V2 card transmits at 27 dBm with a boost converter for its front end, and Heltec publishes no current for it
The draw is a guess (40 mA typical, 80 mA worst) and so is the 4.75 to 5.25 V range. The second CAN plug passes 5 V on to the next node, limited here to the JST-GH contact's 1 A

Fruity Chutes doesn't name the Harrier's trigger servo or its draw. Hitec's HS-55 micro servo stands in: 4.8 to 6.0 V, 5.5 mA idle, 150 mA running, 450 mA stalled (https://hitecrcd.com/hs-55-economy-feather-servo/). Typical is the 0.2 W the sizing model already counts for holding position

No claw design yet. Two servos like Savox's SH-0255MG+ stand in: 180 mA running and 1200 mA stalled at 4.8 V, 240 mA and 1400 mA at 6.0 V (Lindinger's listing of Savox's figures, https://www.lindinger.at/en/RC-ELECTRONICS/Servos-Accessories/Servos-Digital-Low-Voltage/SAVOEX-SH-0255MG-6V-3-9KG-0-13s-Digital-Micro-Servo/9795255). Typical is the 2 W the sizing model counts for holding a grip, split between the two

unproven.what: A dead short in the battery leads. Nothing electrical stops it; only the leads' routing and sleeving protect against it.
unproven.measure: Inspect the leads' routing and sleeving after every crash and every pack change.

unproven.what: The motor cut board's two undocumented 1 kOhm resistors. Check them with a meter; pull-ups would make the board fail the wrong way, which the added pull-down only partly covers.
unproven.measure: Measure them with a meter before the board goes in.

unproven.what: Powering the Pi 5 through its GPIO 5 V pins, which Raspberry Pi's docs don't describe.
unproven.measure: The Pi at full load through its GPIO pins on the bench, its own undervoltage flags logged.

unproven.what: The Pi 5's highest safe input. Raspberry Pi publishes only a 5.1 V supply and the 4.63 V undervoltage warning, so its 5.19 V from the BEC is checked against USB's 5.25 V ceiling, with no margin.
unproven.measure: The BEC's output at the Pi's pins under full load, with a meter; then ask Raspberry Pi.

unproven.what: The ESC cable's re-pinning: Holybro doesn't say which end of its plug is pin 1.
unproven.measure: Find pin 1 with a meter against the ESC's pads before the cable is cut.

unproven.what: Whether the ARK FPV terminates its CAN port. If it does, the harness's terminator at that end comes off.
unproven.measure: CAN_H to CAN_L on the bare board: 120 ohm means it terminates itself.

unproven.what: The XT60's contact mass, a 2.5 g guess. The firmware's heat limit and the burst check both rest on it: heavier contacts give the burst more time.
unproven.measure: Weigh a contact; and the XT60's temperature after a burst, with a thermocouple.
